explanation: The posterior primary rami (dorsal rami) of C2 and C3 supply the skin over the occipital bone up to the vertex, including the greater and lesser occipital nerves.
The masseter muscle develops from the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage), along with other muscles of mastication and mylohyoid.
The thyrohyoid muscle is innervated directly by C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve. Other infrahyoid muscles receive ansa cervicalis (C1-3).
The buccal nerve passes between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid muscle to reach the buccinator muscle, carrying sensory fibers to the cheek.
The uvula deviates AWAY from the lesioned side due to weakness of the palatine muscles on the affected side. Deviation to the right indicates left vagus (CN X) injury.
The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X, XI, and the inferior petrosal sinus. The hypoglossal nerve passes through its own canal (hypoglossal canal) separately.
The common carotid artery typically bifurcates at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4 vertebral level).
The sphenomandibular ligament is the remnant of Meckel's cartilage (first pharyngeal arch cartilage), stretching from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible.
Saying 'No' involves rotation of the head at the atlanto-axial joint (C1-C2), where the dens of the axis articulates with the anterior arch of the atlas.
The mylohyoid muscle develops from the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage), along with other muscles of mastication.

The intermaxillary segment (primary palate) gives rise to the premaxilla, primary palate, and four incisor teeth. The center of the lower lip comes from the mandibular prominence, not the intermaxillary segment.
Early closure of the coronal suture causes brachycephaly (shortened anteroposterior skull diameter) due to compensatory growth in other directions.
Ruffini's corpuscles (type II slowly adapting mechanoreceptors) are proprioceptors in joints and skin. Pacinian corpuscles are vibration/pressure receptors, not proprioceptors.
CNS is NOT rich in connective tissue - it is poor in CT, derived mainly from neuroectoderm. It IS soft and jelly-like (due to high water content), and has grey and white matter.
The anterior horn contains anteromedial, anterolateral, and posterolateral nuclei. There is no 'middle' nucleus in the anterior horn.
Microglia are the resident phagocytic cells of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in CNS injury and disease, acting as macrophages.
Psammoma bodies (laminated calcified concretions) are characteristic of meningiomas, papillary thyroid carcinoma, and serous cystadenocarcinoma of ovary.
Rosette formation (Homer-Wright rosettes) is characteristic of medulloblastoma and other primitive neuroectodermal tumors (PNETs).
Meningiomas show spindle-shaped cells arranged in whorled patterns, sometimes with psammoma bodies. They arise from arachnoid cap cells and can erode skull bone.
Meningiomas characteristically show a whorled pattern of growth with spindle cells and psammoma bodies.
Schwannomas (neurilemmomas) at the cerebellopontine angle show hypercellular (Antoni A) and hypocellular (Antoni B) areas. They arise from Schwann cells.
Ependymomas arise from ependymal cells that line the ventricular system and central canal of the spinal cord.
The posteromarginal nucleus is located in lamina I of the spinal cord and receives pain and temperature afferents from the periphery.
The resting membrane potential (approximately -70 mV in neurons) closely matches the equilibrium potential of K+ (approximately -90 mV) because the membrane at rest is most permeable to potassium.
The crossed extensor reflex is elicited by CONTRALATERAL (not ipsilateral) painful stimulus. The reflex is polysynaptic, has a longer latency than stretch reflex, and involves interneurons.
Increased activity of raphe magnus and locus coeruleus PROMOTES wakefulness and arousal, not sleep. These nuclei are part of the ascending activating system.
Sleep (especially REM sleep) enhances memory consolidation through synaptic reorganization. Anesthesia, concussion, and electroshock impair consolidation.
The enterorhinal cortex (area 28) is the major gateway for neocortical information to hippocampus, critical for forming and retrieving olfactory memories and spatial memory.
Tendon jerks are exaggerated in upper motor neuron lesions (like internal capsule lesion), not Parkinsonism. Parkinsonism has rigidity but normal or slightly brisk reflexes.
GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting on GABA-A receptors to cause chloride influx and hyperpolarization.
Fast pain (A-delta fibers) has a brief duration (~0.1 seconds), occurring immediately after stimulus and enabling rapid localization of noxious stimuli.
Type II (secondary) afferents from nuclear bag and chain fibers in muscle spindles continue firing during slow sustained stretch, unlike rapidly adapting Ia fibers which fire only during changes.
The crossed extensor reflex causes the contralateral extensor to contract when a limb is withdrawn from pain, allowing weight shift and postural support while the affected side flexes.
Buspirone is used for generalized anxiety disorder but lacks efficacy for panic attacks. Panic attacks are typically treated with SSRIs, benzodiazepines, or CBT.
Triazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine; overdose causes prolonged sedation that is reversed by flumazenil. Barbiturates (like pentobarbital) are not reversed by flumazenil.
Infection's acidic environment (low pH) DECREASES the unionized (active) fraction of local anesthetics, reducing their efficacy.
Carbamazepine has a relatively better fetal safety profile than valproate (which causes neural tube defects) and phenytoin.
Bupropion does NOT increase serotonin and has the least sexual dysfunction among antidepressants. Option D (bupropion alone) is correct as it does not induce sexual dysfunction.
Chloramphenicol's most feared adverse effect is aplastic anemia, an idiosyncratic and potentially fatal bone marrow suppression, not anaphylactic shock.
Rifampicin 2-day prophylaxis is used for meningococcal contacts. None of the listed organisms (H. influenzae, S. agalactiae, S. pneumoniae) have this specific prophylaxis regimen.
Riluzole is a glutamate release inhibitor that modestly extends survival and delays ventilator dependence in ALS by reducing excitotoxic neuronal death.
Codeine side effects include constipation (not diarrhea), as it is an opioid constipating effect. It is less potent as an antitussive than morphine.
Ibuprofen is NOT associated with Reye's syndrome (that is aspirin's classic association in children with viral illness). Paracetamol does not cause bleeding.
Piroxicam has a long half-life (50 hours) allowing once-daily dosing, not three times daily.
Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses heroin intoxication by blocking mu-opioid receptors, restoring respiratory drive.
Apomorphine, a dopamine agonist, is used as rescue medication for off akinesia in Parkinson's disease due to its rapid onset when given subcutaneously.
Propranolol (beta-blocker) effectively controls essential tremor and is safe in BPH patients.
Chemical synapse transmission typically has a delay of only 0.3-0.5 msec, not 3-5 msec, due to the rapid release, diffusion, and receptor activation process.
Hypoxia depresses synaptic transmission by impairing the energy-dependent processes required for neurotransmitter synthesis and the Na+/K+ ATPase maintaining membrane potential.
Tissue damage releases kinins (bradykinin, kallidin) which sensitize nociceptors, causing pain as part of the inflammatory response to injury.
Ammonia intoxication symptoms occur when brain ammonia levels are INCREASED (elevated). Normal brain ammonia is kept very low by glutamine synthesis and urea cycle.
Brain glucose uptake is insulin-independent; GLUT1 and GLUT3 are constitutively active at the blood-brain barrier and neuronal membranes.
Brain cells completely oxidize glucose to CO2 and H2O via aerobic metabolism in mitochondria, producing 30-32 ATP per glucose molecule.
Brain uses hexokinase (not glucokinase) to phosphorylate glucose, giving it high affinity for glucose and allowing uptake even at low blood glucose concentrations.
HMP pathway's main importance in brain is generating NADPH for antioxidant defense (via glutathione reductase) and nucleotide synthesis.
5-hydroxytryptophan is decarboxylated by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD) to form serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine).
The phagocytic (inducible) nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is calcium-independent and can be induced by cytokines and endotoxin in macrophages.
Arginine is the only urea cycle intermediate that is incorporated into proteins; ornithine, citrulline, and argininosuccinate are not standard proteinogenic amino acids.
The urea cycle produces fumarate when argininosuccinate is cleaved by argininosuccinase. Fumarate can enter the TCA cycle.
Urea has the formula (NH2)2C=O, containing ONE carbon atom and TWO nitrogen atoms.
The carbon of urea comes from CO2 (as bicarbonate) via carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the mitochondria.
Glutamate provides nitrogen via both glutamate dehydrogenase (oxidative deamination) and glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase (transamination).
Histidine is decarboxylated by histidine decarboxylase to form histamine, analogous to other neurotransmitter synthesis pathways.
Serotonin is synthesized from the essential amino acid tryptophan via hydroxylation (tryptophan hydroxylase) to 5-hydroxytryptophan, then decarboxylation to serotonin.
Carcinoid syndrome diagnosis uses elevated 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid), the main serotonin metabolite, not serotonin itself.
MAO converts serotonin to 5-hydroxyindoleacetaldehyde, which is then oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenase to 5-HIAA.
Decarboxylation of 5-hydroxytryptophan by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD) produces serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine).
Melatonin is synthesized from tryptophan via the pathway: tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan to serotonin to N-acetylserotonin to melatonin.
Urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is the end product of catecholamine catabolism and is elevated in pheochromocytoma.
Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6) is the cofactor for decarboxylation reactions that produce GABA, serotonin, and histamine.
The phagocytic (inducible) nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is calcium-independent and can be induced by cytokines and endotoxin in macrophages during inflammatory responses.
Classic PKU causes deficiency of both catecholamines and melanin due to tyrosine deficiency (tyrosine is an essential dietary requirement in PKU).
Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting on NMDA, AMPA, and kainate receptors.
Pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-secreting tumor) causes elevated urinary VMA (vanillylmandelic acid), the main metabolite of epinephrine and norepinephrine.
